items.stem: In an exothermic reaction, the enthalpy change ΔH is:
items.note: Exothermic: products lower in energy than reactants → ΔH < 0, heat released to the surroundings (container feels warm).

items.stem: On an energy profile, the activation energy is the distance from:
choices: Reactants to the peak of the curve
items.note: Ea = energy difference between reactants and the transition state (peak). ΔH is reactants-to-products — two different arrows on the same diagram.

items.stem: A catalyst speeds up a reaction by:
items.note: A catalyst provides an alternative route with lower Ea — the energy profile's peak drops, but ΔH stays exactly the same.

items.stem: Which process is endothermic?
choices: Neutralisation of an acid by an alkali
items.note: Melting/evaporation absorb energy to break intermolecular forces. Combustion, neutralisation and respiration release energy.

items.stem: 100 g of water absorbs 4.18 × 10³ J and its temperature rises by 10.0 K. This is consistent with a specific heat capacity of:
items.note: q = mcΔT → c = q/(mΔT) = 4180/(100 × 10.0) = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ — the value to quote from the data booklet for water.

items.stem: In a calorimeter, an acid–alkali reaction causes the solution temperature to rise. The reaction is therefore:
items.note: Rising solution temperature = energy released by the reaction = exothermic = negative ΔH. The sign is the most-loses-mark detail in these calculations.

items.stem: Hess's law states that the enthalpy change of a reaction:
choices: Is independent of the route taken, depending only on initial and final states
items.note: Enthalpy is a state function — which is why energy cycles work: indirect routes give ΔH values that cannot be measured directly.

items.stem: The bond enthalpy of H–Cl is defined as the energy:
choices: Released when H–Cl forms in solution
Required to break one mole of H–Cl bonds in the gaseous state
Released per mole of HCl formed from elements
items.note: Two conditions matter: gaseous state, and one mole of bonds. Bond enthalpies are averages — they differ slightly from measured values in real molecules.

items.stem: Using average bond enthalpies (H–H 436, Cl–Cl 242, H–Cl 431 kJ/mol), ΔH for H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl is:
items.note: ΔH = bonds broken − bonds formed = (436 + 242) − 2(431) = 678 − 862 = −184 kJ/mol. Remember to multiply by the number of each bond type.

items.stem: In an exothermic reaction, the energy released on bond formation is:
choices: Less than the energy absorbed in bond breaking
Greater than the energy absorbed in bond breaking
items.note: Every reaction breaks then forms bonds: exothermic = forming releases more than breaking costs. Endothermic is the reverse.

items.stem: Which species has a standard enthalpy of formation, ΔH·f°, equal to zero by definition?
items.note: An element in its standard state (here O₂ gas at 100 kPa, 298 K) is assigned ΔH·f° = 0 — the reference point of energy cycles.

items.stem: Which change causes an increase in entropy?
choices: Sublimation of dry ice (solid CO₂ → gas)
Precipitation of a solid from solution
items.note: Entropy rises with disorder: gas > liquid > solid. Going solid → gas is the biggest jump; freezing/condensing/precipitating all lower it.

items.stem: For the reaction 2SO₃ → 2SO₂ + O₂, ΔS is positive because:
choices: The number of moles of gas increases from 2 to 3
items.note: Count gaseous moles: 2 → 3 means more ways to arrange the particles — positive ΔS. State symbols decide entropy, not oxidation numbers.

items.stem: A reaction is spontaneous when:
items.note: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS < 0 defines spontaneity. Negative ΔH alone doesn't guarantee it, and positive ΔS alone doesn't prevent it — temperature decides.

items.stem: A reaction with ΔH negative and ΔS positive is:
items.note: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS: both terms push ΔG negative → spontaneous at every temperature. The other three sign combinations are temperature-dependent.

items.stem: An endothermic reaction with positive ΔS becomes spontaneous:
items.note: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS: the favourable TΔS term can only outweigh positive ΔH when T is large enough. Melting ice is the everyday example.

items.stem: Enthalpy is best described as:
choices: The heat energy stored in a system at constant pressure
The total bond energy of all bonds
items.note: Enthalpy (H) is measured as heat exchanged at constant pressure — which is why calorimetry and ΔH live together.

items.stem: In the equation q = mcΔT, the mass m should be:
choices: The mass of the reactant added
The mass of the solution absorbing the heat
The molar mass of the product
items.note: The thermometer sits in the solution — m is everything the water/solution heats (usually solution mass ≈ volume in g). Using only the solute's mass is a classic error.

items.stem: If a temperature DECREASES is recorded for a reaction mixture, the reaction was:
items.note: Falling temperature = the mixture drew heat from its surroundings = endothermic → positive ΔH. Read the sign from the thermometer's direction.

items.stem: When ΔG = 0, the system is:
choices: At equilibrium / the reaction is neither spontaneous in either direction
items.note: ΔG = 0 marks the equilibrium point — the balance between enthalpy and entropy drive. Below it forward, above it reverse.

items.stem: 50.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol/dm³ HCl is mixed with 50.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol/dm³ NaOH. The temperature of the mixture rises by 6.50 K. Calculate the enthalpy change of neutralisation per mole of water formed (c of the solution = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹; assume the density of the solution is 1.00 g/cm³).
markscheme: Mass of solution = 100.0 g (both volumes, density 1.00) (1)
ΔH = −2.72/0.0500 = −54.3 kJ/mol — negative because temperature rose (1)
items.tactic: Neutralisation calorimetry: total solution mass, q = mcΔT, divide by moles of WATER formed (not acid), sign from the thermometer. −54−57 kJ/mol is the accepted range.

items.stem: For a reaction, ΔH = +50.0 kJ/mol and ΔS = +100 J/K/mol. Determine the temperature above which the reaction becomes spontaneous.
markscheme: Convert ΔS to kJ: +100 J/K/mol = +0.100 kJ/K/mol (1)
Interpretation: entropy-driven reaction, only spontaneous at high temperature (1)
items.tactic: The unit conversion (ΔS in J vs ΔH in kJ) is where most marks die — convert first, then solve the inequality, then interpret in words.

items.stem: In an exothermic reaction, the products have:
choices: Less energy than the reactants — ΔH is negative
The same energy as the reactants
items.note: Energy is released to the surroundings: products sit LOWER on the energy profile. ΔH = H(products) − H(reactants) < 0.

items.stem: On an enthalpy level diagram, the activation energy is measured from:
choices: Reactants to the peak of the curve
items.note: Ea = reactants → transition state (peak). ΔH = reactants → products. Two different arrows — examiners ask for both by name.

items.stem: A catalyst speeds up a reaction by:
choices: Providing an alternative pathway with lower Ea
items.note: The catalyst offers a lower-Ea route — more collisions succeed. ΔH and the equilibrium position are unchanged.

items.stem: Which process is endothermic?
items.note: Melting absorbs energy to overcome intermolecular forces. Combustion, neutralization and respiration all release heat.

items.stem: In a calorimetry experiment, 100 g of solution rises 6.5 K. Using c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹, the heat released is approximately:
items.note: q = mcΔT = 100 × 4.18 × 6.5 = 2717 J ≈ 2.7 kJ. The mass is the WHOLE solution — not just the solute.

items.stem: Hess's law allows enthalpy changes to be calculated indirectly because enthalpy is a:
choices: State function — independent of the route
items.note: ΔH depends only on initial and final states. Energy cycles combine routes: ΔH₃ = ΔH₁ + ΔH₂ with signs reversed as needed.

items.stem: ΔH for a reaction from bond enthalpies is calculated as:
items.note: Breaking absorbs (+), forming releases (−): ΔH = Σ(broken) − Σ(formed). Gaseous state required for all bond enthalpies.

items.stem: A reaction has ΔH > 0 and ΔS > 0. It becomes spontaneous:
choices: Only at high temperatures, where TΔS outweighs ΔH
items.note: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS < 0 needs TΔS > ΔH — only large T delivers that for an endothermic, entropy-increasing reaction (e.g. melting ice above 0 °C).
